ABSTRACT  
It has become crucial to investigate the uncertainty and sensitivity of building loads (peak cooling load, peak 
heating load, annual cooling demand and annual heating demand) for meeting the risk assessment of building 
energy planning. Therefore, a new Monte Carlo (MC) method based on building performance simulation (BPS) is 
proposed to solve the problem of building loads forecasting at planning phase. Furthermore, the sensitivity of 
building loads is examined using two global sensitivity analysis (GSA) methods, including meta modeling method 
based on tree Gaussian process (TGP) and regression method based on standard regression coefficient (SRC). 
Finally, a case study of office building is conducted. The results show that the MC method constructed by the 
combination of R language platform and EnergyPlus software can generate models rapidly and simulate accu -
rately building loads. Note that it is necessary to assess the stability of results as a function of sample size from 
uncertainty analysis in applying the MC method into building loads assessment. The TGP-based GSA method is 
applicable to identify and analyze key variables affecting building loads. It is recommended that at least two 
inherently different GSA methods should be applied to provide robust sensitivity results. Moreover, this study 
also provides insight on building energy planning and energy conservation design according to the results of 
uncertainty and sensitivity analysis for case study.   
1. Introduction 
Building energy planning is an effective way to reduce building en -
ergy consumption under the premise of ensuring the safety of building 
energy use [ 1 – 3 ]. As the first step of the planning, cooling/heating load 
calculation is very significant because it will affect the energy system 
configurations. At the planning stage, due to the lack of detailed archi -
tectural design scheme, the following two calculation methods are 
usually used to predict the building cooling/heating load. One is the 
area index method [ 4 ], another is deterministic building performance 
simulation (BPS) using professional platform (such as EnergyPlus, 
DOE-2, TRNSYS, and DeST). In order to ensure the energy system to 
have sufficient capacity, the common practice is to multiply the 
maximum load with a safety factor. Since the choice of an adequate 
safety factor is highly dependent on the designers ’ experience, the 
resulting variation in the robustness of the system could be large. To 
avoid the responsibility of under-sizing, the safety factor is often larger 
than that actually needed. So the system is usually oversized, together 
with high capital cost and low operational efficiency. Therefore, it is 
necessary to carry out uncertainty analysis (UA) in the characteristics of 
cooling and heating loads at the planning stage to appropriately size 
equipment and reduce energy consumptions. 
UA has been widely implemented in various areas of building energy 
analysis, including model calibration [ 5 , 6 ], load forecasting [ 7 – 9 ], 
impact and adaptation to climate change [ 10 – 12 ], sensitivity analysis 
(SA) [ 13 , 14 ], spatial analysis [ 15 , 16 ], and optimization [ 17 – 19 ]. 
Several studies have focused on uncertainty quantification of cooling 
and heating loads. Domínguez-Munoz et al. [ 20 ] proposed a probabi -
listic approach to consider the uncertainty of input factors influencing 
peak cooling load. Twenty uncertain factors are considered to calculate 
peak cooling load using a simple lumped heat-balance model. Sun et al.

[21] further explored the heating ventilation and air conditioning 
(HVAC) sizing issues for both cooling and heating loads using UA, which 
can replace the safety factor commonly used in HVAC industry. This UA 
of cooling and heating loads takes into account actual observed weather 
data and provides rich probabilistic information on cooling and heating 
demands to support risk-based sizing. Lin Lin et al. [22] simulated and 
calculated the cooling load of a typical hub airport terminal on the basis 
of UA. The result shows that compared with the given parameters, more 
accurate average probability distribution and peak load distribution of 
terminal cooling load can be obtained under uncertainty parameters. 
While UA and SA is closely related, they belong to two different 
disciplines. UA is focused on either assessing output uncertainty derived 
from input uncertainty or obtaining input uncertainty from measure -
ment data, whereas SA concentrates on assessing the contributions of 
input factors for variations of system outputs. SA plays an important role 
in building energy analysis. It can be used to identify the key variables 
affecting building thermal performance from both energy simulation 
models and observational study. SA can be divided into two main cat -
egories, local and global [23]. A local sensitivity analysis (LSA) evalu -
ates the response of the model to one local parameter. Global sensitivity 
analysis (GSA) explores the response of the model to changes in all input 
parameters, which are varied simultaneously [24]. GSA provides more 
information about the effect of varying model inputs but demands more 
computational effort. GSA can be further subdivided into four categories 
[25]: regression, screening, variance-based and meta-models. Many 
variables affecting cooling and heating loads are uncertain at the plan -
ning stage and the impact of these uncertainties is the reason for limiting 
the simulation accuracy. 
The meta modelling method for GSA is a new one among these 
methods and consists of two steps: firstly construct a meta-model from 
detailed dynamic BPS; then implement a variance-based method using 
this meta-model [26]. The meta-models, also called surrogate models, 
are statistical models which approximate the objective function using 
the design of computer experiments [27]. The variance-based sensitivity 
method is to determine the contributions of individual factors to the 
variance of the output. This method is appropriate for non-additive 
non-linear model because of its model independence [24]. The combi -
nation of meta-models and variance-based method has several 
advantages in comparison with other approaches for SA. Firstly, it needs 
less simulation runs compared to variance-based method because the 
disadvantage of variance-based SA is very time-consuming for engi -
neering models and the meta-models have low computational cost. 
Secondly, it is suitable for complicated relationships between inputs and 
outputs due to the use of variance-based method, while the regression 
methods are appropriate for linear or monotonic models. Thirdly, it can 
quantify output variances due to every input, whereas the screening 
methods are usually only for qualitative purpose. Furthermore, the 
method can incorporate the uncertainty of both function outputs and 
integral estimation for sensitivity index, which are rarely used in most of 
SA methods [28]. Lastly, the method has a visual tool to show how the 
model output responds to every input factor [28], which can be very 
useful to show whether there are linear or non-linear relationships in the 
models. 
Previous researches have not often focused on the uncertainty 
quantification of the four indicators of peak cooling load, peak heating 
load, annual cooling demand and annual heating demand at the plan -
ning stage. Moreover, the methods used in the previous studies are 
usually simplified models, which will bring additional model uncer -
tainty to the uncertainty quantification of building loads. However, 
these building loads may have a critical impact on system design ca -
pacities for meeting the risk assessment of building energy planning. 
Therefore, the purpose of this paper is to construct a building loads 
forecasting method framework suitable for the lack of detailed building 
information in the building energy planning stage, and quantify the 
uncertainty of peak cooling load, peak heating load, annual cooling 
demand and annual heating demand using the proposed method 
framework to serve the practice of building energy planning. 
Furthermore, previous studies have almost ignored the SA of peak 
cooling and heating loads to input parameters, especially the related 
elements of architectural design. Therefore, another aim of this paper is 
to implement GSA to identify and analyze key variables influencing peak 
cooling load, peak heating load, annual cooling demand and annual 
heating demand. More specifically, this paper examines the implications 
of the sensitivity of the different parameters for each result using meta 
modeling method based on TGP and regression method based on SRC.

an office building, which can provide insight on energy demand from the 
perspectives of total energy demand and system capacity for building 
energy systems, respectively. This study would also be helpful to identify 
cooling and heating design best practices for office buildings to guide

The paper consists of the following sections: Section 2 presents the 
proposed methodology including MC method based on BPS, UA method, 
meta modeling method based on TGP and regression method based on 
SRC. In Section 3 , a case study of building energy model is described in 
detail. In Section 4 , the sample size for UA and SA is analyzed selected, 
the uncertainty of peak cooling load, peak heating load, annual cooling 
demand and annual heating demand is quantified, and the main factors 
contributing to these four indicators are identified and analyzed using 
two GSA methods. Finally, the paper is closed with conclusions. 
2. Methodology 
The most important link for UA and GSA is to choose a method of 
uncertainty propagation. A MC method based on BPS constructed by the 
combination of R language platform and EnergyPlus software is pro -
posed in this paper. This method has two main advantages: one is that a 
large number of models can be generated quickly by the combination of 
R language platform and EnergyPlus software and the interface of BPS 
model is easy to understand and operate; another is that compared with 
the uncertain input parameters, the mature EnergyPlus software used in 
this paper can ignore the uncertainty brought by the model, which can 
provide more accurate data for UA and GSA of building loads. The 
specific implementation process of the UA and GSA on the basis of the 
proposed new MC method is illustrated in Fig. 1 . 
2.1. MC method based on BPS 
2.1.1. Step 1 Specify distributions of input factors 
The first step of MC method based on BPS is to specify distributions of 
input factors, including certain factors and uncertain factors. This step is 
both the most important and the most difficult task. For the certain 
factors, specific design values are determined according to standards 
and codes. As shown in Fig. 1 , the factors from x

tribution, uniform distribution, etc. It should be noted that Gaussian 
distributions need to be truncated where necessary to avoid unfeasible 
values (for instance, a negative value or zero for length-width ratio of 
building). 
2.1.2. Step 2 Generate samples and combinations 
The second step is to generate samples with Latin hypercube sam -
pling (LHS) and combine the input factors. LHS used in this paper is a 
very popular method suitable for computationally demanding models

due to its stratification properties [ 15 ]. In short, LHS divides the range of 
every input variable into N segments (the specific sample size) with 
equal probability. The recommended length of the segments is depen -
dent on the specified probability distribution shapes of input variables. 
One value is then randomly selected from each segment until all seg -
ments have one sample. An important feature in the LHS is that every 
hypercube partitioned by segments associated with input variables has 
the same number of samples. The general recommendation for a LHS 
sample size is ten times the number of variables in computer experi -
ments [ 27 ]. However, this sample size may be inadequate for UA when 
complicated non-linear relationships between inputs and outputs exist 
in the cooling and heating loads models. Therefore, further research will 
be carried out in this paper to provide clear guidance on the sampling 
number suitable for the UA and GSA. LHS is implemented here using R 
software. Finally, a matrix X with m rows (sample size) and n columns 
(number of input factors) is generated by combining the certain and 
uncertain factors, as shown in Fig. 1 . 
2.1.3. Step 3 Create and run loads forecasting models 
The third step is to automatically create building loads forecasting 
models using R software and run the models by EnergyPlus software. A 
large number of simulation runs are usually required in UA. Hence, it is 
necessary to automate the generation of simulation models with 
different input values, the simulation of models, and the extraction of 
the relevant data from simulation results using computer programming 
languages or specialized tools. In this paper, R software can use the input 
samples from the previous step to write the EnergyPlus models because 
the Input Data File (IDF) file required for EnergyPlus is an ASCII (i.e. 
text) file, which can be easily edited in the R language environment 
[ 29 ]. In order to reduce the time cost, EnergyPlus models are run on a 
multi-core computer and R platform is used again to automatically read 
the outputs from a large number of simulation runs in this paper.

mathematical problems by performing statistical sampling experiments

for input factors and generate a probability distribution for each output 
[ 30 ].

Uncertainty quantification can be presented as numerical values or 
as visual graphs. Numerical indicators are descriptive statistical mea -
sures including mean, median, standard deviation and percentile etc. 
Typical graphical methods include frequency distribution, Q-Q plot, 
probability density function (PDF), cumulative distribution function 
(CDF) and box plots etc. Frequency distribution shows that the data can 
be represented by some kind of distribution curve with a satisfactory fit. 
More specifically, this approach involves fitting a histogram based on 
output data with a suitable PDF. Q-Q plot demonstrates in how far the 
distribution matches the assumptions by means of a normality plot. Its 
purpose is to graphically assess whether the data follows a normal dis -
tribution. Box plots are used to show the quartile map. More valuable 
information can be provided based on PDF and CDF plots, such as 
confidence level and probability to exceed a threshold value. In this 
paper, the outputs of cooling and heating loads will be quantified by 
both numerical values and graphs. 
2.3. TGP-based GSA method 
The meta-modelling of GSA based on Treed Gaussian Process (TGP) 
will be used to identify and analyze the key variables affecting cooling 
and heating loads. TGP is one of the state-of-art machine learning 
methods, developed by Gramacy [ 31 ]. TGP couples stationary Gaussian 
process with treed partitioning, so it provides a flexible and powerful 
nonparametric and nonstationary regression model. And this method 
was further developed by Gramacy et al. [ 28 ] to be suitable for SA. The 
GSA method based on TGP can be implemented by R tgp package, which 
was developed by Gramacy for R software [ 29 ]. Compared to other types 
of meta-model SA, the meta-model GSA based on TGP incorporates two 
types of variations for sensitivity index: uncertainty on function outputs; 
variability from integral estimation [ 31 ]. 
Two sensitivity indices can be provided by the meta-model GSA 
based on TGP: first order and total effects. The first order is to represent 
the main effect contribution of each input variable to the variance of the 
output. In contrast, the total effects is to represent the total contributions 
to the output variance due to each input factor by considering main 
effects and all higher-order effects. Therefore, the difference between 
the first order and total effects for one input variable indicates the in -
teractions between this variable and other variables. The R tgp package 
provides fully Bayesian non-stationary non-linear models (called treed 
Gaussian processes, TGP) and contains the sensitivity index calculation 
functions based on variance method. The functions allow for easy 
calculation of two very important sensitivity indices associated with 
each input: the first order for the jth input variable, as shown in formula

3. A case study of building loads model 
3.1. Building conditions 
As shown in Fig. 2 , it is known that an office building will be built on 
the planning site (blue dashed box) in Tianjin, China. The plot ratio of 
the planned office building is 8, the building density is no more than 0.4, 
and the building height is limited to no more than 160 m. Other detailed 
planning information are shown in Table 1 .

3.4. Model generation 
After defining all the parameters required by the building loads 
model, the LHS method is used to sample eleven uncertain parameters. 
Then, a complete reference model of high-rise office building is estab -
lished in the form of code on the R language platform, in which the 
uncertain parameters are defined as variables and other deterministic 
parameters are set as fixed values. Finally, the code is used to iterate the 
uncertain parameter values in each sample into the reference model, and 
the IDF format model recognized by EnergyPlus software is automati -
cally generated. As shown in Fig. 7 , four building loads models with 
different parameter values are automatically generated. 
4. Results and discussion 
4.1. Sample size analysis 
Before conducting the UA and GSA, it is necessary to select the 
appropriate sample size to make the simulation results stable. The time 
cost and simulation accuracy caused by sample size is an inherent 
contradiction, so the determination of sample size needs to compromise 
these two aspects. In this paper, four percentiles (25th, 50th, 75th, and 
95th) of peak cooling load, annual cooling demand, peak heating load 
and annual heating demand are proposed as monitoring values to 
determine the sample size. Starting with 55 samples, gradually increase 
the number of samples, and observe the fluctuation of simulation results. 
Each group of samples generated a considerable number of prediction 
models, so a total of 45210 models are generated in this study. 
As can be seen from Fig. 8 , the peak heating load and annual heating 
demand converge faster than the peak cooling load and annual cooling 
demand. However, under the same sample size after convergence, the 
relative error of cooling loads is smaller than that of heating loads. The 
percentiles of peak cooling load, peak heating load, annual cooling de -
mand and annual heating demand become approximately stable after

5. Conclusions 
The deterministic building loads predictions only provide limited 
confidence for building energy planning. As these forecasting models 
involve many input parameters, the uncertainty introduced by each 
parameter may invalidate the entire simulation result. Therefore, the 
needs for uncertainty quantification and key factors identification of 
building loads at planning phase is quite evident. In this paper, the UA 
and GSA of peak cooling load, peak heating load, annual cooling de -
mand and annual heating demand are studied in building energy plan -
ning stage. The main conclusions can be summarized as follows:  
(1) A new MC method based on BPS has been proposed to solve the 
problem of building loads forecasting at planning phase. The MC 
method constructed by the combination of R language platform 
and EnergyPlus software provides a new idea for rapid generation 
of models and accurate simulations of building loads. Note that it 
is necessary to assess the stability of results as a function of 
sample size from uncertainty analysis in applying the forecasting 
method into building loads assessment. This is often ignored in 
applying UA in the field of building loads analysis. The relative 
errors of the output percentiles are used as the basis for the se -
lection of sample size in this paper.  
(2) The TGP-based GSA method is applicable to identify and analyze 
key variables affecting building loads. For the method, besides 
the point estimate of sensitivity index, the variations of these 
sensitivity measures can be also created to provide more robust 
analysis. Furthermore, the method can also show the main effects 
of varying each input on outputs, including the trend of outputs 
change due to the corresponding input. Furthermore, it is rec -
ommended to compare several SA methods and then choose at 
least two applicable methods that are inherently different in na -
ture in order to provide robust analysis. 
(3) For the case study of office building in this paper, some conclu -
sions can be drawn. Peak cooling load, annual cooling demand, 
peak heating load and annual heating demand all follow normal 
distributions. The key factors affecting above four outputs are 
different, including two aspects of importance ranking and pos -
itive and negative correlation. These four outputs are mainly 
driven by main effects and the interaction terms are not signifi -
cant, and the relationships between key inputs and outputs are 
approximately monotonic and linear. Moreover, this study also 
provides insight on capacity design for building energy planning, 
and the energy system with large demand differences should be 
carefully decided based on the combination of uncertainty and 
sensitivity analysis. 
It is worth noting that the very limited range means the impact of the 
building envelope on the energy demand does not change much due to 
over-insulation, one can be lead to believe that the U-values do not 
impact the results, but this is only because the variations are so small. 
Therefore, in order to achieve building energy conservation, we should 
not always blindly pursue to improve the thermal performance of 
building envelope. When the thermal performance of building envelope 
reaches a certain level, its improvement on building energy conservation 
will be greatly reduced. Compared with other measures, the advantage 
of improving its performance may be not obvious. On the contrary, the 
cost will increase sharply. Therefore, the range of variables is also very 
important when performing sensitivity analysis. Maybe the same vari -
ables have very different effects on the results in different ranges. This is 
also an interesting point for future research.
